name: Richard R. Burton
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. BS Caltech 1970 (~22); PhD UC Irvine 1976 (~28) for AI tutoring work (SOPHIE et al.) largely completed in mid-20s but major dated recognition and PARC career (joined 1978, ~30) and ACM Software System Award for Interlisp (1992) came after 26.
early_history_summary: Born 1948 in Oakland, CA to teacher parents. Earned a BS in mathematics from Caltech in 1970, then pursued AI tutoring research with John Seely Brown at UC Irvine and Bolt Beranek and Newman, completing a PhD in 1976. Joined Xerox PARC in 1978; later managed HCI research and co-received the ACM Software System Award for Interlisp.
family_context_summary: Grew up as the child of two teachers; education was emphasized at home. Further family financial detail not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were teachers; not documented as computer-science domain experts.
evidence_summary: Burton's best-known contributions—intelligent tutoring systems with Brown at BBN and later Interlisp/PARC leadership—are dated primarily from the mid-to-late 1970s onward. Caltech graduation at ~22 is education, not a material breakout; PhD and SOPHIE-era papers land around age 27–28; PARC hire at ~30. No clear, independently dated material milestone at or before 26 established.

name: Dennis Ritchie
milestone_by_age_26: Major material achievements (Unix ~1969–1970, C language early 1970s) occurred after age 26. Joined Bell Labs Computing Sciences in 1967 at ~25–26 and worked on Multics, but C and Unix—the defining milestones—came at ~28–31.
early_history_summary: Born 1941 in Bronxville, NY; father Alistair E. Ritchie was a Bell Labs scientist. Graduated Summit High School and earned Harvard degrees in physics and applied mathematics (1963). Joined Bell Labs in 1967, collaborated with Ken Thompson on Multics then Unix, and created the C programming language.
family_context_summary: Father Alistair E. Ritchie was a longtime Bell Labs scientist and co-author of switching-circuit work; family lived in Summit, New Jersey.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a Bell Labs technical staff member in switching circuit theory—direct domain proximity to industrial research computing.
evidence_summary: Ritchie's legendary impact is undeniable, but the dated material milestones (Unix development with Thompson ~1969–70 at age ~28–29; C language development early 1970s at ~30+) fall after age 26. Bell Labs hire in 1967 is notable employment at an elite lab but is not treated here as the breakout material milestone comparable to inventing C/Unix.

name: Aaron Patterson

early_history_summary: Known online as tenderlove; prominent Ruby and Rails core contributor and author of widely used libraries (e.g., Nokogiri, Psych). Has worked at Red Hat/ManageIQ, GitHub, and Shopify as a senior/staff engineer focusing on Ruby runtime and Rails performance.
evidence_summary: CSV lists birth year 1978. Publicly documented core-team milestones and major library authorship that made him widely known occur in the late 2000s–2010s, after age 26. No independently dated ≤26 breakout found in reviewed sources.

milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Born ~1979 (Forbes age 46 as of 2025); taught himself Ruby ~2007 (~28); encountered/commercialized GitLab ~2012 (~33); GitLab Inc. founded 2014 (~35); IPO 2021.

evidence_summary: GitLab's founding and commercialization—the material founder milestones—occurred in Sid's early-to-mid 30s, well after age 26. Pre-26 record lacks a dated, material public breakout in reviewed sources.

name: Bjarne Stroustrup
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Cand.scient. Aarhus 1975 (~24) is a degree; PhD Cambridge 1979 (~28); began C with Classes / C++ at Bell Labs in 1979 (~28–29); C++ generally available 1985 (~34–35).
early_history_summary: Born 1950 in Aarhus, Denmark to a working-class family. Studied at Aarhus University (1969–1975) learning microprogramming and OOP concepts via Kristen Nygaard visits; PhD Cambridge 1979 under David Wheeler; joined Bell Labs 1979 and invented C++.
family_context_summary: Working-class family in Aarhus, Denmark; attended local schools. Further parental occupation detail limited in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as computer-science domain experts.
evidence_summary: Stroustrup's defining achievement—design and implementation of C++—began at Bell Labs in 1979 when he was about 28–29, after age 26. Education milestones before 26 do not constitute the material breakout under this rubric.

name: Isaac L. Auerbach
milestone_by_age_26: Joined the Eckert–Mauchly Computer Corporation (later Univac) as a research engineer in 1947 at age 25–26 and helped design BINAC (contract signed Oct 9, 1947—his 26th birthday) and UNIVAC I as part of the original team for the first commercial electronic digital computers.
early_history_summary: Born 1921 in Philadelphia; BS electrical engineering Drexel 1943; US Navy service in WWII sparked deeper computing interest; MS applied physics Harvard 1947. Immediately joined Eckert–Mauchly to design early stored-program machines, then managed computer product work at Burroughs (1949–1957) before founding Auerbach Associates and Auerbach Publishers and serving as founding president of IFIP (1960–1965).
primary_leverage_engine: Scarce technical depth at computing's birth
secondary_engine: Frontier geography / first commercial computer ecosystem
family_context_summary: Born in Philadelphia; early family financial and parental occupation details not richly documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Eckert-Mauchly, BINAC, UNIVAC, Drexel, Harvard, Philadelphia computing hub
evidence_summary: Auerbach entered the absolute frontier of electronic computing by joining Eckert–Mauchly in 1947 at age 25–26 and contributing to BINAC/UNIVAC design. IEEE Computer Society pioneer materials and multiple historical sources place him on the original team. He later founded consulting and publishing firms, led IFIP as founding president, earned 15 patents, and was elected to the National Academy of Engineering. Family advantages are weakly documented; leverage mainly came from scarce early computer-engineering skill plus proximity to the Philadelphia commercial computer cradle.
starting_point: Born in Philadelphia in 1921; educated at Drexel (BSEE 1943) and Harvard (MS applied physics 1947) after WWII Navy service.
current_position: Died December 24, 1992 at age 71 in Lower Merion, Pennsylvania; final roles included computer industry entrepreneur, IFIP founding president, and National Academy of Engineering member.

trajectory.event: Joined Eckert–Mauchly as research engineer and began design work on BINAC (contract Oct 1947) as part of the original commercial electronic computer team.
Co-authored the mercury delay-line memory paper; completed BINAC-era engineering; moved to Burroughs to manage defense/space computer products.
Founded Auerbach Associates, widely cited as the first dedicated computer consulting firm.
Became founding president of the International Federation for Information Processing (IFIP).
Elected to the National Academy of Engineering for pioneering computing contributions.
Died in Lower Merion, Pennsylvania; IFIP later established an award in his name.

name: Tom Hall
milestone_by_age_26: Lead designer on Commander Keen (first episode released as shareware Dec 14, 1990) and co-founded id Software on February 1, 1991 at age 26 with John Carmack, John Romero, and Adrian Carmack.
early_history_summary: Born September 2, 1964 in Wisconsin; parents brought home an Apple computer in 1980, which he lived on. Earned a BS in computer science from University of Wisconsin–Madison (class of 1986). Joined Softdisk in 1987 as programmer and disk-magazine editor, then moonlit with Carmack and Romero on Commander Keen before formally founding id Software in 1991.
primary_leverage_engine: Product / design taste with high-trust cofounders
family_context_summary: Raised in Wisconsin; parents provided an Apple computer in 1980 that catalyzed intensive early practice. Broader family wealth/status not detailed in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as game-industry or software professionals; provided early home computer access.
primary_early_advantage_tags: id Software, John Carmack, John Romero, Softdisk, Commander Keen, shareware, UW-Madison
evidence_summary: Tom Hall combined early personal-computer practice, a CS degree, Softdisk game work, and an exceptional cofounder set (Carmack/Romero) to ship Commander Keen and incorporate id Software at 26. He was creative director/designer on Keen, Wolfenstein 3D, and early Doom before leaving id in 1993, later co-founding Ion Storm (Anachronox/Deus Ex era) and continuing design work into the 2020s. Family domain advantage is limited; leverage is peer team, product taste, and the PC shareware wave.
starting_point: Born in Wisconsin in 1964; middle-class-leaning household that gave him an Apple computer in 1980; CS degree from UW–Madison.
current_position: Living game designer affiliated with Romero Games and prior design work including VR title Demeo; maintains thattomhall.com; co-founder of id Software and Ion Storm.

trajectory.event: Joined Softdisk as programmer and editor of the Softdisk disk magazine, entering professional game/software production.
Lead designer on Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons, released as shareware via Apogee on December 14, 1990.
Co-founded id Software (February 1, 1991) with John Carmack, John Romero, and Adrian Carmack.
Creative director on Wolfenstein 3D, a breakthrough first-person shooter that defined id's commercial path.
Left id Software during Doom development after design disagreements; joined Apogee/3D Realms.
Co-founded Ion Storm with John Romero; later designed/produced Anachronox and contributed to Deus Ex.
Released Anachronox as project leader/game designer at Ion Storm.
Continued design work including contributions to VR tabletop RPG Demeo; remains active as an independent/affiliated designer.
